nameStory: The veiled panus gets its name from the distinctive partial veil that covers young mushrooms like a tiny curtain. This veil is quite unusual among small, stemless mushrooms, making it stand out from other wood-dwelling fungi. The word 'panus' comes from Latin meaning 'swelling' or 'tumor,' referring to its bulbous appearance on decaying wood.
description: The veiled panus is a small, humble brown mushroom that grows directly on rotting hardwood without a visible stem. These inconspicuous fungi appear in tight clusters or scattered groups, looking like tiny brown buttons dotting dead branches and logs. Young specimens are covered by a delicate partial veil that eventually breaks away as the mushroom matures. They're quite small, rarely exceeding an inch across, making them easy to overlook during casual woodland walks.

idTips.label: Partial Veil
idTips.description: Young mushrooms have a thin, web-like veil covering the cap that breaks apart as they mature - this is the key identifying feature since no other stemless mushrooms have this veil

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Small, dull brown caps that feel smooth and slightly leathery when touched, often with a shallow depression in the center like a tiny bowl

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: No visible stem - mushrooms attach directly to the wood surface, sometimes with a very short, stubby base

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Always found in clusters or scattered groups on dead hardwood, never growing singly or on the ground

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Mild, earthy mushroom smell without any distinctive or unpleasant odors

idTips.label: Safety Note
idTips.description: Never eat wild mushrooms without expert identification - these small brown fungi can be easily confused with other species

habitat: Look for veiled panus on decaying logs, fallen branches, and dead wood of broad-leaved trees throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. They particularly favor oak, maple, beech, and birch wood that's been dead for at least a year. You'll find them from lowland forests up to mid-elevation woods, wherever hardwood debris accumulates in moist, shaded areas.

seasonality.spring: Early fruiting begins as the soil warms and spring rains provide moisture to decaying logs. Look for the distinctive veiled young specimens emerging from winter-weathered hardwood.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when warm, humid conditions after summer thunderstorms trigger abundant mushroom production. This is the best time to observe the characteristic partial veil on fresh specimens.
seasonality.fall: Continued fruiting through early autumn, especially during the wet season. Older specimens may lack veils but clusters are still visible on logs.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting bodies die back, though dried remnants may persist on logs. The fungus continues decomposing wood internally, preparing for next year's growth.

funFact: The veiled panus is like a botanical unicorn - it's the only small, stemless mushroom in New England that sports a partial veil, making it surprisingly easy to identify despite its plain brown appearance once you know what to look for!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small brown mushrooms growing on wood, but the partial veil on young specimens is a dead giveaway. Memory trick: 'Veiled and stemless' - no other wood-dwelling mushroom in our region combines these two features.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name including 'panus,' this mushroom was recently moved from the genus Panus to Tectella based on genetic studies. You may still find it listed as Panus patellaris in older field guides, which can cause confusion for beginning mycologists.
compareHints: Since it's the only Tectella species in New England, compare it with other small, wood-dwelling mushrooms in the broader agaric family. Unlike oyster mushrooms or other bracket fungi, it has true gills and that distinctive partial veil. It's much smaller than most Panus species and lacks their characteristic tough, leathery texture when mature.
